newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian call ends up on less supply, gilts down.
newsitem.headline: Indian call ends up on less supply, gilts down.

text.p: Indian call money firmed up on shortage of funds to end the last trading day of 1996/97 (April-March) at 6.5 percent, dealers said.
They said call money opened Monday at 4.25-5.0 percent and eased to 4.0-4.25 percent in early trade before an unexpected shortage of funds pushed rates up.
"It was a little unexpected," said a dealer at a state-run bank. "It appears some lending banks went out of the market on capital adequacy considerations."
He said these banks had not lent out of fear they would have to provide capital against their assets.

"It is a bit confusing...I am not why sure capital adequacy should have prevented banks from lending today," he added. "But some lending banks stopped lending in late morning itself citing this reason."
Dealers said prices of government securities fell in light trade.
"I think some banks may have sold securities today to raise cash as supply of funds dried up and call money rates rose," said a dealer. "Prices generally fell today."

The 13.50 percent 1997 traded on Monday at 101.48 rupees against its last traded 101.55, the 13.50 percent 1998 dropped to 103.20 from 103.24 and the 12.50 percent 2004 eased to 96 from 96.04, dealers said.
In other securities, treasury bills maturing in July traded steady at 9.35 percent while Septmeber bills were unchanged at 9.5-9.65 percent, dealers said.
The treasury bill auctioned last Wednesday at 10.12 percent traded on Monday at 10.18 percent, dealers said.
The money market is inactive on Tuesday as banks are shut for public transactions for annual accounting purposes.
